title: The Church and the Poor at the Door
subtitle: On mercy ministry done with dignity, the biblical call to the poor, and how a congregation serves the needy without wounding them

sections.title: The Knock the Church Dreads
sections.body:
Every church has a back door, and sooner or later someone knocks on it who does not look like the congregation. The man with the gas can story. The mother with three kids and an eviction notice. The veteran who smells of the street.

The staff sighs. The receptionist tenses. And in that small reflex, the church reveals what it actually believes.

We have made the poor an interruption to the ministry instead of seeing that they are the ministry. Jesus did not place the poor at the edge of his work. He placed them at the center, and he warned us, in the plainest terms he ever used, that on the last day he would ask what we did with the hungry and the imprisoned and the stranger, and that he would receive our answer as if we had done it to him. I have been the man who hoped the knock would stop. I am not proud of it. The church that learns to dread that knock has quietly stopped being the church and become a club with a steeple.

sections.title: This Is Not Optional Charity
sections.body:
We treat care for the poor as a nice extra, a thing generous churches do when the budget allows. The Bible treats it as a test of whether you know God at all.

He defended the cause of the poor and the needy, the prophet says of a good king. Was that not what it means to know me, says the Lord.

The theme runs from the law to the prophets to the lips of Jesus to the practice of the first church, where they sold their possessions so that no one among them was in need. You cannot cut it out of Scripture without cutting out most of Scripture. A gospel that saves your soul and ignores your starving neighbor is not the gospel the apostles preached. James said it with a knife. Faith that sees a brother without clothes and food and says go in peace, be warm and filled, and gives him nothing, is dead. So this is not the soft side of ministry to be funded last. It is near the heart of the thing, and a church that misses it has missed something it cannot afford to miss.

sections.title: Help That Does Not Humiliate
sections.body:
It is possible to give bread and take dignity in the same motion, and churches do it constantly without meaning to. The handout delivered with a faint disgust. The charity that makes the giver feel large and the receiver feel small. The program that treats the poor as projects to be processed.

Look a poor man in the eye. Learn his name. Sit down with him before you reach for your wallet.

The poor are not a category. They are people, each with a face and a history and a dignity that poverty has bruised but not erased. Real mercy asks before it acts. It listens to what the person actually needs instead of imposing what is convenient to give. It walks alongside rather than tossing aid from a distance. And it refuses the lie that the poor are poor because they are lazy and the comfortable are comfortable because they are righteous, a lie the rich have always found convenient. Give in a way that you would be willing to receive. If the help would shame you, it will shame him. Mercy that wounds is not mercy. It is contempt with a receipt.

sections.title: Compassion Needs a Spine
sections.body:
Soft hearts are not enough. The poor are served badly by a church that hands out cash with no thought and calls the carelessness love.

Real help is harder than a check. It asks more of you than your money.

There is a kind of giving that relieves the giver's guilt while keeping the receiver stuck, that funds an addiction or rewards a con and feels holy doing it. Wisdom distinguishes the emergency from the pattern, the crisis that needs cash from the chaos that needs a long relationship and a firm hand. Connect the person to the church family, not just to the benevolence fund. Walk with them toward work, toward sobriety, toward a stability that outlasts the next crisis. This is slower and far more costly than writing a check, which is exactly why most churches prefer the check. But the poor were never helped by money alone. They are helped by people who will stay long enough for the help to take. Give your money. Then give the harder thing, which is yourself.

sections.title: The Poor Are Already in the Pews
sections.body:
We picture the poor as someone outside, a stranger at the door, and miss the ones already sitting in our rooms. The single mother stretching the offering she cannot afford. The old man choosing between medicine and the gas to get to church. The family one paycheck from the street, dressed well enough that we never asked.

The poor are not only at the door. They are in the third row, and we have trained them to hide.

We built churches so comfortable that the struggling learned to mask their struggle to belong, and in doing so we made our own brothers invisible. The early church knew its poor by name and made sure none went hungry. We often do not even know who ours are. So look closer at the people you already have before you congratulate yourself on a program for people you do not. Make a church where it is safe to be poor, where need is met without spectacle, where no one has to perform prosperity to be loved. The Lord who became poor for our sake is not far from the back door. He is also in the third row, waiting to see if we will notice him.
